children.text: A brackish lake hidden behind the limestone cliffs of Coron Island. Fresh water and seawater separate in the shallows, and around 14m deep the temperature climbs to nearly 38℃, an unusual underwater world that divers rank among their favorites, while snorkelers can still see the submerged cliffs.
Barracuda Lake is a brackish lake trapped among the limestone peaks of Coron Island in northern Palawan. It sits near the north shore of Coron Island, about
5km

in a straight line from Coron town, between Kayangan Lake and Twin Lagoon. After stepping off the boat and following wooden stairs and boardwalks over sharp limestone, you suddenly face a lake whose gray cliffs drop straight to the water's edge. On the surface it is perfectly still, but underneath it hides layers you will hardly find anywhere else.
What made this lake famous worldwide is its upside-down temperature. Most lakes get colder as you go deeper, but here the water near the surface is about
and then, at around
, suddenly heats up to nearly
. Higher up, at about
4m

, fresh water above meets seawater below, forming a halocline where the boundary shimmers like a heat haze. The warm deep water is often attributed to geothermal heat, but the exact cause is not clear. The maximum depth is said to be about
, and the bottom is fine silt your hand sinks right into.

The name is said to come from a story that the bones of a huge barracuda were found in the lake, or from a legend that a single giant barracuda once lived here. Seeing a barracuda today is rare, and with few fish it is not as colorful as a coral reef. Instead, there are records of small shrimp, gobies and catfish among the rocks. Coron Island is the ancestral land of the indigenous Tagbanwa people, and since this lake was opened to visitors together with Kayangan Lake in
, the community has managed its entrance fees and rules. Locally it is also known as Luluyuwan.
For scuba divers it is a rare experience to pass through fresh water, seawater and a hot layer in a single dive, and since the water is clear with visibility often reaching

, freedivers love it too. Even with just a snorkel you can clearly see the submerged limestone cliffs and rock ridges, so it suits any traveler who enjoys swimming. It is part of the Tour B route, which is less crowded than Kayangan Lake, so it is also good for those looking for a quiet lake.
The moment you pass about

and the water turns as hot as a bath is the lake's signature experience. You go in on a guided dive with a dive shop, and the temperature change you feel going down and coming up is big, so move slowly.

blocks.title: Seeing where fresh water meets salt

children.text: At the halocline, around
4m
deep, the water looks warped like glass. Stir it with your hand and watch the two waters mix, blurring your view before it clears again.
Right below the surface, the limestone cliffs drop straight into the depths. Just floating face down in a life jacket reveals an underwater scene of rock textures and blue light.
With almost no waves or current and clear water, the lake is known as a good place to practice freediving. Always go in with an instructor or a buddy, and never go alone beyond the designated area.

blocks.title: Climbing the wooden stairs through limestone

children.text: From the sea-side landing to the lake, wooden stairs and boardwalks wind between knife-edged limestone.
5–10 minutes
is enough to get up and down, but the cliff views between the rocks are already worth it.

Climb down from the lake-side deck into the water and swim along the cliffs. The lake is deep and you can hardly touch bottom anywhere, so wear a life jacket, lie back on the water and look up at the gray cliffs all around.

blocks.title: The fine silt on the lake floor

children.text: Divers can go down near the bottom and feel the soft silt their hands sink into. Deeper down, silt and compounds from fallen leaves cloud the water, so stay close to your guide.

items.title: Joiner Tour B
items.subtitle: The easiest option for swimmers and snorkelers

children.text: Get picked up at your hotel in Coron town and head to the pier.
The tour boat departs. Tour B usually combines Barracuda Lake, Twin Lagoon, Skeleton Wreck, a coral garden and Smith Beach.
Arrive at Barracuda Lake and cross the wooden stairs to the lake. Swim and snorkel for about
1 hour
Move to nearby Twin Lagoon and try crossing between the two lagoons.
Have lunch prepared by the boat crew on a beach.
Snorkel at Skeleton Wreck and a coral garden.
Return to the pier in Coron town.
The order of stops changes depending on the operator and the day's tides. Visiting Barracuda Lake first means fewer people, so ask about the order when you book.

items.title: Half-day dive trip
items.subtitle: When you want to pass through the thermocline yourself

children.text: Meet at the dive shop, get fitted for gear and attend the briefing. Bring your certification card and recent logbook.
Leave on the dive boat and reach the landing at the lake entrance after about
20–30 minutes
Carry your tank and gear over the wooden stairs and enter the water from the lake-side deck.
Enjoy a
40–50 minute
dive through the halocline and thermocline.
Rest on the boat, then make a second dive at a nearby wreck or reef.
Return to Coron town or continue with afternoon wreck dives.

items.title: Early-morning private boat
items.subtitle: When you want the lake to yourself

children.text: Leave the Coron town pier on a private bangka booked the day before.
Arrive at the lake ahead of the group tours. Check the lake's opening time on site.
Snorkel and swim in the calm lake, and take photos of the cliffs from the water.
Move on to Twin Lagoon or Kayangan Lake, or head back to town before the crowds.

items.title: From Coron town to the lake

children.text: The only way to the lake is by sea. A boat from the Coron town pier takes about
20–30 minutes
to reach the small cove at the lake entrance, and from the landing it is
5–10 minutes
over the wooden stairs to the lake.
Joiner tour: included in Tour B and the Super Ultimate tour, at about
per person. Hotel pickup and lunch are usually included.
Private boat: about
for the whole group, and you can set the departure time and order of stops.
Diving: the lake is part of day dive trips run by dive shops in Coron town.
Northern Palawan, where Coron lies, has a dry season from
December–May
and a rainy season from
June–November
. In the dry season the sea is calm for boat trips, and sunlight reaches deep into the lake, making the water and cliffs look their sharpest.

Because the lake is enclosed by cliffs and barely touched by wind or waves, divers say conditions underwater hardly change through the year. The problem is the sea crossing to get there. When a typhoon approaches in the rainy season, the coast guard stops boats from sailing and tours are canceled entirely, so leave some slack in your schedule.

The best time of day is early morning, before the group tour boats arrive. The fewer people in the water, the calmer the surface, so the submerged cliffs look clearer and the shimmer of the halocline is easier to see.

Coron Island, where the lake is, is Tagbanwa land, so there is no lodging on the island and visitors must leave before dark. Staying in Coron town across the water and commuting by boat is the norm. Near the pier in the town center you will find dormitories (about
per night) and guesthouses (about
), while mid-range hotels run about
. If you plan to dive, stay in the center where the dive shops are clustered, which makes early-morning meetups easier.

There are no restaurants or shops at the lake, so keep water and snacks on the boat. Tour lunches are typically fish and pork the crew bought at the market, grilled over charcoal and served with rice and fruit on a beach or on the boat. After the tour, many travelers head to seafood restaurants in Coron town in the evening for the day's catch, grilled squid and kilawin (raw fish cured in vinegar).
For a quiet lake, check whether your Tour B stops at Barracuda Lake first, or hire a private boat early in the morning.
The entrance fee is about
and is often included in joiner tour prices. On private boats or dive trips you may pay it separately, so bring cash.

The thermocline lies below 14m, so it is hard to feel when snorkeling. To feel the hot water yourself, go scuba diving or freediving; snorkelers can enjoy the shimmering boundary in the shallows and the cliffs.

If you plan to dive, bring your certification, and since your buoyancy changes as temperature and salinity shift, adjust your weights with your guide in advance. Without certification, ask the dive shop whether they offer discover scuba dives here.
Wet wooden stairs and rocks are slippery, and limestone edges are razor sharp. Wear aqua shoes with firm soles.
Snorkel gear and aqua shoes are often not included in tour prices. Check rentals when you book or bring your own.
Bring a waterproof camera for underwater photos. The halocline blurs the focus, so shooting above and below the boundary shows the difference clearly.
To protect corals and wildlife, use reef-safe sunscreen and keep oily products on your skin to a minimum before entering the lake.
Much of the lake is deeper than

, so you lose your footing just a short way from the edge. Weak swimmers and children must wear life jackets and stay within sight of the guide. Entry rules and fees can change by community decision, so check the latest notices before you visit.
The hot water below the thermocline can be unsettling the first time. Always dive with a local guide, and if you feel unwell, ascend to shallower water right away.
In the depths, stirred-up silt can wipe out visibility in an instant. Don't kick the bottom, and don't drift away from your guide.
Never freedive alone. There have been accidents from overambitious dives in Coron Island's lakes, and life jacket rules have become stricter as a result.
This is the ancestral domain of the Tagbanwa people. Leave no trash, stick to the designated decks and stairs, and follow the caretakers' instructions.
Don't fly right after diving. It is safest not to schedule dives the day before you leave Coron.
